 Federal loan changes could affect Texas State students
 Sidney Orman , News Reporter 
 November 11, 2026 
 Kaliyah Riley 
 A federal policy may restrict access to federal student loans for certain college programs whose graduates continue to earn below the federal government’s earnings benchmark.
 The  U.S.  Department of Education  announced a new rule on June 29 under the  Student Tuition and Transparency System  (STATS) and Earnings Accountability, where if the graduate’s earnings are under the benchmark, the current students enrolled in the program could have their federal student loan availability restricted.
 Undergraduate programs will be compared with the median earnings of working adults with a high school diploma, while graduate programs will be compared with working adults who hold a bachelor’s degree.
 “Under the new Student Tuition and Transparency System (STATS) and Earnings Accountability rule, undergraduate programs will be required to demonstrate that their graduates earn more than the typical high school diploma holder, and graduate programs will be required to demonstrate that their graduates earn more than the typical bachelor’s degree holder,” the Department of Education wrote in a press release in June.
 According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, full-time workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma makes  $977 in median weekly earning in 2026,  while a bachelor’s degree holder makes  weekly wages of $1,541  in 2024.
 If a program fails to show financial return on investment for its graduates in two out of three consecutive award years, it will lose eligibility for the federal Direct Loan program. After three years of consistently failing, the program could also terminate eligibility for Title IV of the Higher Education Act (HEA), including Pell Grant eligibility, for all of an institution’s low-earning outcome programs, according to the  Department of Education. 
 “Amid rising rates of default and delinquency in the $1.7 trillion federal student loan portfolio, this new accountability framework is a responsible policy that will safeguard American taxpayer dollars and protect students from taking on unmanageable debt for programs that cannot demonstrate a reasonable return on investment,” Under Secretary of Education Nicholas Kent said in the Department of Education press release.
 James Petrovich, director of social work, said once he learned about the new policy he thought about the challenges students could face if they lose access to their federal loans.
 “I think there’s a lot more expensive schools out there, but that doesn’t mean it’s not expensive for an individual,” Petrovich said. “Loans have made higher education accessible for a lot of people who would not have been able to get to it otherwise, so I think there’s value in that.”
 LeeAnn Partin, communication design junior, relies on federal student loans to continue her education. Partin said without the necessary loans to keep her enrolled at Texas State, it could mean lots of uncertainty for her future.
 “As a student who uses loans, it makes me very nervous to think about not being able to continue my education,” Partin said. “I completed my associate’s degree already, and it was a big financial choice for me to decide to go to university.”
 Federal loans are made by the U.S Department of Education, with terms and conditions set by law, including interest rates and income-driven repayment plans, while private loans are made by private organizations such as banks and credit unions. Private loans are generally more expensive than federal student loans and often not subsidized, according to  Federal Student Aid. 
 Partin’s major is housed under Texas State’s School of Art and Design, where, according to the Education Initiative data, new bachelor’s degree graduates in  Design and Applied Arts  have a median student loan debt of $28,641 across Texas.
 Petrovich said it is important to set students up for success.
 “One of my goals as an educator is to make sure that when students leave our program, they have a good career in front of them,” Petrovich said. “I want them to have a good life. I want them to make a good wage. I want them to feel fulfilled in what they do as a social worker.”
 The majority of the rule will be in full effect July 1, 2027 including the new earnings accountability requirements, according to the  Federal Update .
 Petrovich said he hopes Texas State will do its part in ensuring students are prepared for what might happen next.
 “I think that just means the university has to do a really good job to help our students get good jobs,” Petrovich said.
